old.name: Villa Noailles
old.hook: Robert Mallet-Stevens' 1920s modernist villa above Hyères, now an art centre, with a triangular Cubist garden and two summer festivals born inside it.
old.text: Robert Mallet-Stevens' 1920s modernist villa above Hyères, now an art centre, with a triangular Cubist garden and two summer festivals born inside it. Charles and Marie-Laure de Noailles, the most reckless art patrons of their day, handed the young Robert Mallet-Stevens a hillside and asked for 'an interesting little house to live in.' In successive campaigns from 1923 to 1933 he answered with a white, cubic manifesto of the Modern Movement: indoor pool, gymnasium, squash court, and a triangular Cubist garden built in 1926-27 by Gabriel Guévrékian, once crowned by Jacques Lipchitz's bronze 'La Joie de Vivre,' which rotated on its base every four minutes. The couple bankrolled the avant-garde with the same open hand: Buñuel's scandalous L'Age d'Or and Man Ray's 'Les Mystères du Château du Dé' (shot here in 1929) were their money. Hyères took the house over in 1973; today it hosts the two events it spawned, the Hyères International Festival of Fashion & Photography (founded 1985 by Jean-Pierre Blanc, then 21, and now the oldest young-designer fashion competition in the world) and Design Parade. The one real thing to carry away: this is where modernism learned it was allowed to be joyful, not just severe. Signal Built in campaigns 1923-1933 by Robert Mallet-Stevens; municipal art centre since 1973; Design Parade held 25-28 June 2026

old.name: Fondation Carmignac (Villa Carmignac)
old.hook: A contemporary-art foundation buried under a restored Provençal farmhouse on a car-free national-park island, walked barefoot.
old.text: A contemporary-art foundation buried under a restored Provençal farmhouse on a car-free national-park island, walked barefoot. Financier and collector Édouard Carmignac sank a 2,000 m² gallery beneath an old mas and a ceiling of water on the protected island of Porquerolles, opening it in 2018. You leave your shoes at the door and cross the galleries barefoot before spilling into a fifteen-hectare garden studded with sculpture. Because Porquerolles is a national park, you arrive only by boat and there are no cars, so the art is framed by umbrella pines, salt air and heat-shimmer instead of white walls. Verified: the 2026 show 'Sea, Pop & Sun' (curated by Dieter Buchhart and Anna Karina Hofbauer, setting Warhol, Lichtenstein and Martial Raysse against living artists) runs 25 April to 1 November. The real thing to know: it borrows its title from a summer mood and is engineered to feel like a daydream rather than a museum. Signal Opened 2018 by Édouard Carmignac; 2026 exhibition 25 Apr-1 Nov

old.name: Domaine du Rayol — Le Jardin des Méditerranées
old.label: ~50 min east on the Corniche des Maures
old.hook: A twenty-hectare seaside domain whose gardens landscape philosopher Gilles Clément replanted from 1989 with the floras of every Mediterranean-climate zone on earth — California, Chile, South Africa, South Australia — tumbling to a turquoise cove.
old.text: A twenty-hectare seaside domain whose gardens landscape philosopher Gilles Clément replanted from 1989 with the floras of every Mediterranean-climate zone on earth — California, Chile, South Africa, South Australia — tumbling to a turquoise cove. Clément's 'garden in movement' made concrete: no clipped parterres, just curated wildness, managed ecologically. Owned by the Conservatoire du Littoral. The same coast road strings past Bormes-les-Mimosas and, further east, the hill villages of Gassin and Ramatuelle.

old_also.name: Domaine du Rayol, Le Jardin des Mediterranees
old_also.hook: 20 hectares of protected coast (7 of garden, 13 of maquis) facing the Port-Cros islands, with a grand antique-style pergola and cypress-lined stair down to the sea and, in summer, a guided snorkel trail in the bay.
old_also.text: 20 hectares of protected coast (7 of garden, 13 of maquis) facing the Port-Cros islands, with a grand antique-style pergola and cypress-lined stair down to the sea and, in summer, a guided snorkel trail in the bay. The Conservatoire du littoral rescued the abandoned estate in 1989 and handed it to landscape gardener Gilles Clement, who refused a manicured garden and instead planted a mosaic of the world's other Mediterranean climates: South African fynbos, Chilean matorral, Californian chaparral, Australian kwongan and mallee, all thriving under the same Var sun. The monumental pergola was raised around 1910 for the estate's first owner, the Parisian businessman Alfred Courmes; the aviator Henri Potez, who bought the domain in 1940, later drove the long cypress-lined stair down through it. Terroir made literal, and gardened without irrigation or pesticides from the start. Signal Pergola built c.1910 for Alfred Courmes; estate bought by the Conservatoire du littoral 1989; garden conceived by Gilles Clement.

old.name: Village des Tortues, Carnoules
old.hook: A 2-hectare sanctuary and veterinary clinic at the foot of the massif where you walk among Hermann's tortoises: rescue, breeding pens, incubation and a release programme.
old.text: A 2-hectare sanctuary and veterinary clinic at the foot of the massif where you walk among Hermann's tortoises: rescue, breeding pens, incubation and a release programme. The Maures and the neighbouring Plaine des Maures hold the last wild population of Hermann's tortoise on the French mainland. Naturalists Bernard Devaux and David Stubbs founded the SOPTOM association in 1986 and opened the first village at Gonfaron on 28 May 1988; it moved to its current Carnoules site in June 2017. The one real thing it teaches: France's only native land tortoise survives essentially here, and its two great killers are summer wildfire and the roads that cut its range. Signal SOPTOM founded 1986; village opened 28 May 1988 (Gonfaron); relocated to Carnoules June 2017.

old.label: Lorgues
old.hook: The one genuinely third-wave, Anglophone-style operation in the Var. old.name: Sénéquier
old.text: The red-awninged café-institution on the old port. The Sénéquier name dates to 1887, when Marie and Martin Sénéquier opened a pâtisserie (famous for a nougat recipe of the same year) at the Place aux Herbes; the business expanded to the quayside, where it became a café in 1930. Destroyed by bombardment in 1944 and rebuilt by 1951, its scarlet director's chairs and triangular tables are the town's front-row seat for watching the port — and everyone from fishermen to passing celebrities has taken one. The honest truth You pay tourist-port prices for a coffee, but the bill is really rent on the best people-watching terrace in Saint-Tropez. In August it is packed and priced to match. Signal A Sénéquier institution since 1887 (pâtisserie at Place aux Herbes); a quayside café since 1930, rebuilt after the war and reopened in 1951. Still trading.

old_also.name: Sénéquier
old_also.hook: The red-chaired café on the quay, an open-air observatory of the port since the age of the New Wave.
old_also.text: The red-chaired café on the quay, an open-air observatory of the port since the age of the New Wave. Sénéquier began as a patisserie founded in 1887 by Marie and Martin Sénéquier, pastry-makers already famous for a white nougat of Spanish almonds, Sicilian pistachios and Provence honey. In 1930 Lisette Sénéquier turned it into a café and tea room on the harbour, and its unmistakable bright-red tables and chairs became the front row for the Nouvelle Vague and everyone after. Bombed in 1944 and rebuilt by 1951, its thirty-metre terrace of director's chairs and triangular tables is still the most conspicuous seat on the quay. The real thing: order a drink here and you are paying for a sightline, not the glass, it is the most famous café on the Riviera precisely because it faces the whole promenade of the port. Signal Patisserie founded 1887 (Marie & Martin Sénéquier); harbour café from 1930; rebuilt 1951; landmark red terrace
